The median is the reference because it is the one statistic the explosion never moves: in Fig. 2b the median and the 99.9th percentile stay flat through the update that halts SHAC, and only the maximum leaves.
Clipping touches 9–21% of the samples, i.e. of the (step, environment) pairs, per update, removes the tail of Fig. 2a and leaves the rest of the batch unchanged.

abstract:
Robot policy learning is dominated by zeroth-order methods such as PPO, which treat the simulator as a black box and pay for it with enormous sample counts. First-order policy learning differentiates through the dynamics, but on contact-rich whole-body control it has rarely worked: its gradients explode. A recent world-model method showed that derivative information can make humanoid motion tracking far more efficient, using surrogate gradients of a learned model. We show that exact gradients of the simulator itself do better, once two obstacles are removed. Exact gradients contain rare unbounded samples, because contact dynamics is not differentiable everywhere and its derivative diverges near some events; and they are expensive, because the simulator’s adjoint has to replay the contact solve.

$\nabla$Mimic bounds these samples with median-relative per-sample gradient clipping at every step of the backward pass, and reuses each costly simulated window by multistep regression onto gradient-derived action targets, which bounds every action target independently of the gradient scale. NablaEngine, a differentiable GPU simulation engine for the Unitree G1, removes the cost: it computes MuJoCo’s full contact dynamics with fused per-world kernels and the adjoint of a whole control step as a single megakernel, with analytic gradients that match float64 finite differences, $11.5\times$ faster than the available MuJoCo Warp adjoint.

On whole-body tracking of all 40 LAFAN1 clips with one policy on one GPU, $\nabla$Mimic reaches the score reported by the state-of-the-art world-model method, 0.82, in 20 minutes instead of 1.2 h, and 0.874 in 1.8 h. SHAC, the standard first-order baseline, stops on exploding gradients within minutes. We release NablaEngine and $\nabla$Mimic as open-source infrastructure for first-order humanoid policy learning.

sections.body: The paper trains a humanoid motion-tracking policy with first-order gradients taken from the simulator itself, after removing two obstacles: rare unbounded gradient samples and the cost of the adjoint. ∇Mimic bounds per-sample gradients with median-relative clipping and reuses each simulated window through multistep regression onto gradient-derived action targets. NablaEngine computes the Unitree G1 contact dynamics and an analytic adjoint on the GPU. On all 40 LAFAN1 clips, with one policy on one GPU, ∇Mimic reaches 0.82 in 20 minutes, where SuperMimic reports 1.2 h, and 0.874 in 1.8 h. PPO on the same engine stays below 0.82 for 6 h.
sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.headline: Exact simulator gradients, with two obstacles removed, match the world-model score for humanoid tracking in minutes instead of hours.

sections.body: Prior work falls into four groups. Zeroth-order PPO trackers, such as BeyondMimic and SONIC, use black-box rewards and large sample counts. First-order methods such as SHAC use short backpropagation-through-time windows with a critic, and some legged-robot methods smooth contact to keep gradients finite. Gradients through learned world models, as in SuperMimic, come from a surrogate system rather than the simulator. On the engine side, MuJoCo Warp has no differentiable release, and its adjoint exists only in an open pull request. The section places this work against these groups: exact gradients of the simulator, clipped per sample inside the backward pass, on an engine built for the G1.
sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.headline: Prior work uses zeroth-order PPO, short first-order windows, smoothed contacts or learned models, but not exact full-contact simulator gradients.

sections.body: The task is whole-body motion tracking on the Unitree G1 with 29 actuated joints, using the mjlab model. Control runs at 50 Hz with 4 physics substeps of 5 ms. The policy observes a 10-frame history of noisy proprioception, the next 10 reference frames, and the orientation of the reference anchor body, without global position. The reward follows BeyondMimic's tracking terms over 14 bodies, with action-rate and joint-limit penalties. An episode terminates when the root height error exceeds 0.25 m or the tilt error exceeds 0.8. The return of a window of H steps is differentiated through the dynamics by backpropagation through time, so the quality of the gradient depends on the quality of the derivatives.
sections.heading: 3 Background
sections.headline: Tracking on the G1 is posed as a windowed return whose pathwise gradient depends on the dynamics' derivatives.

sections.body: Exact simulator gradients are unbiased but unbounded near non-differentiable contact events. The self-contact normal's derivative grows as the inverse of the distance between the feet, and on training windows the gradient grew by up to 4.9×10^21 through a window. A surrogate gradient from a multilayer perceptron world model is bounded everywhere by a Lipschitz constant, but it describes a different system and is biased. The two gradients agree on most samples and differ in the tail. Exact derivatives are also expensive, because the adjoint replays the contact solve. In SHAC's raw gradients, one sample reaches 2.2×10^9 times the batch median, which is why per-sample handling and a cheaper adjoint are both needed.
sections.heading: 4 Exact and surrogate gradients
sections.headline: Exact simulator gradients are unbounded in rare samples and costly, while world-model gradients are bounded but biased.

sections.body: ∇Mimic is a windowed first-order actor-critic with two components. Per-sample median-relative clipping caps each action cotangent at κ times the batch median norm, with κ=3, at every backward step. Multistep regression then turns each clipped gradient into an action target whose RMS setpoint change is a fixed δ in radians, and fits the policy to the targets with several minibatch steps. In LAFAN1 ablations with absolute actions, against a control of 0.855, removing clipping diverged one of three seeds, and the other two reached 0.562. One Adam step per window instead of multistep regression gave −0.049. Residual actions reached 0.82 in 0.34 h, against 0.50 h with absolute actions. The section notes that clipping biases the clipped samples and does not quantify this bias.
sections.heading: 5 $\nabla$Mimic
sections.headline: Per-sample clipping and multistep regression onto gradient-derived targets keep exact gradient updates bounded.

sections.body: NablaEngine simulates the G1 with MuJoCo's full contact model, 502 contact pairs and Newton constraint solver, mapping one world to one warp. The forward step runs as two fused kernels per substep, and the adjoint of a whole control step is a single megakernel. The backward pass is derived by hand and differentiates the constraint solve through its optimality conditions, with discrete decisions held fixed. Analytic gradients match float64 finite differences of MuJoCo to 10^-5 in median relative error. For training, the derivatives of near-touching self-contact normals and near-parallel capsules are frozen. A step with its gradient takes 1.78 ms, against 1.21 ms for the step alone, so the adjoint adds 0.57 ms.
sections.heading: 6 NablaEngine
sections.headline: NablaEngine runs the full G1 contact dynamics and its adjoint in one megakernel, 11.5× faster than the MuJoCo Warp adjoint.

sections.body: One policy trains on all 40 LAFAN1 clips on one RTX PRO 6000, and each clip is scored by its full-clip normalized return. ∇Mimic reaches 0.82 in 20 min and 0.874 in 1.8 h, with no seed falling on any clip from 1.5 h on. PPO in BeyondMimic's configuration reaches 0.64 after 3 h, and SHAC stops on its gradient guard at 0.06 h. With the guard relaxed, SHAC reaches 0.816 after 3 h and stays just below 0.82. SuperMimic enters through its stated numbers, since its implementation is not public. On the MuJoCo Warp adjoint with the same algorithm, per-update curves overlap, and NablaEngine is 4.7× ahead per hour. Several baselines are single seeds.
sections.heading: 7 Experiments
sections.headline: ∇Mimic reaches 0.82 in 20 min and 0.874 in 1.8 h, while PPO reaches 0.64 after 3 h and SHAC halts at 0.06 h.

sections.body: The engine supports one robot, the G1, on flat ground. Other robots need their own kernels, and uneven terrain needs height fields and more collision types. Results are on LAFAN1 in simulation only, with no hardware deployment and no training on larger motion libraries. The gradient holds the discrete contact decisions fixed, so it is exact almost everywhere rather than smoothed across contact changes. Per-sample clipping biases the clipped gradients, and this bias is not quantified. The PPO baselines and the MuJoCo Warp run are single seeds. SuperMimic's implementation is not public, so the comparison uses its stated numbers on a different GPU. Extending the engine, scaling to larger libraries and transferring to real robots are the next steps.
sections.heading: 8 Limitations and future work
sections.headline: Results cover one robot on flat ground, in simulation on LAFAN1, with single-seed baselines and unquantified clipping bias.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the two obstacles: rare unbounded samples in the gradient and the cost of computing it. NablaEngine removes the cost for the G1, with an adjoint that costs less than another forward step. ∇Mimic bounds the rare extreme samples with per-sample clipping and reuses each costly window through multistep regression. Together they train one policy that tracks all 40 LAFAN1 clips and reaches the world-model score of SuperMimic in 20 minutes on one GPU. The authors argue that this reduction from hours to minutes makes training on larger and more diverse motion corpora practical, which could accelerate the scaling of humanoid foundation models.
sections.heading: 9 Conclusion
sections.headline: Cutting tracking training cost from hours to minutes could make larger motion corpora practical for humanoid foundation models.

sections.body: The appendix gives task details, including the reward terms, the observation layout and the domain randomization. It describes the engine's model, kernel structure, tape and constraint-solve adjoint, along with the gradient modes and the unbounded-derivative cases. It also covers determinism and the timing protocol. Later tables give the full component ablations, training-loop cost per policy update for each simulator, and the step and gradient times of other engines.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists task and reward details, engine kernel and adjoint derivations, timing protocol, and extended ablation and cost tables.
